sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Root cause analysis (RCA) is the structured post-incident process of reconstructing the timeline, identifying the proximate and contributing causes, and producing actionable items that prevent recurrence — while treating the incident as a learning opportunity rather than a blame opportunity.
Root cause analysis is what happens after an incident is mitigated: the system is back up, users are no longer being harmed, and the team has a window (typically 24–72 hours) to figure out what happened, why, and how to prevent it from happening again. The output is a postmortem document that contains a timeline of events, a list of causes (not "the" cause, because incidents almost always have multiple contributing causes), and a set of action items with owners and due dates. The process matters as much as the output: a blameless, structured RCA produces learning and improvement; a blameful, ad-hoc RCA produces defensiveness, hidden failures, and recurring incidents. The discipline of RCA is the discipline of treating every incident as a symptom of a system-level weakness, not a personal failing of an engineer.

The foundational concept is the blameless postmortem, a practice formalized by Etsy's John Allspaw and adopted by Google, Netflix, and the SRE community. The rule is simple: the postmortem meeting is a blame-free zone. Engineers who made the mistake that triggered the incident (pushed the bad config, ran the destructive query, deployed the broken code) are present and speak freely, because the assumption is that they did what any reasonable engineer would have done given the information and tools they had. The fault is in the system — the deploy process that allowed the bad config, the access controls that allowed the destructive query, the test suite that did not catch the broken code — not in the engineer. The reason this matters is not altruism but engineering: blameful postmortems cause engineers to hide future incidents, which prevents learning, which guarantees recurrence. Allspaw's framing: "a postmortem is a learning opportunity, and the engineer who triggered the incident is the most important person in the room, because they know more about what happened than anyone else." Netflix's postmortem culture goes further: they publish postmortems internally with full detail, run "postmortem-of-the-postmortem" reviews to improve the RCA process itself, and treat blamelessness as a non-negotiable engineering value.

The second concept is the 5 Whys technique, borrowed from Toyota's manufacturing quality system. The technique is to ask "why?" five times in sequence, each answer becoming the premise of the next question, walking from the symptom (the user-visible harm) down to the root cause (the systemic weakness that allowed the symptom to occur). The example from the SRE book: (1) Why did the user see an error? Because the database rejected the write. (2) Why did the database reject the write? Because the schema validation failed. (3) Why did the schema validation fail? Because a column was missing. (4) Why was the column missing? Because the migration was not run. (5) Why was the migration not run? Because the deploy process did not include a migration step. The root cause is "the deploy process did not include a migration step," and the action item is "add migration to the deploy process," not "the engineer forgot to run the migration." The discipline of 5 Whys is to keep asking until the answer is a system-level weakness that, if fixed, would prevent not just this incident but a class of similar incidents. The failure mode is stopping too early — "the engineer made a mistake" is not a root cause, because it does not suggest a system-level fix; the team must keep asking why the engineer was able to make the mistake, why the system did not catch it, why the deploy process allowed it through.

The third concept is the fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram, a structured brainstorming tool for identifying contributing causes across categories. The diagram has a central horizontal arrow pointing to the symptom (the incident), with diagonal "bones" labeled by category — People, Process, Technology, Environment, Measurement, Materials (or a system-specific variant like Code, Config, Capacity, Network, Dependencies). Each bone is populated with contributing causes identified by the team. The fishbone is useful when 5 Whys would produce a single linear chain and miss parallel contributing causes — most incidents have several (the deploy was misconfigured AND the alert did not fire AND the on-call was not paged AND the rollback was slow), and the fishbone surfaces them all. The fishbone's value is breadth: it forces the team to consider every category rather than fixating on the most obvious one. The discipline is to populate the fishbone with verifiable causes (each backed by evidence), not speculation.

The fourth concept is timeline reconstruction. The postmortem must include a precise, evidence-backed timeline of what happened, when, and who did what — from the first event that contributed to the incident (often hours or days before the user-visible symptom) through detection, response, mitigation, and resolution. The timeline is built from logs, metrics, alert history, chat transcripts, and the on-call engineer's recollection; it is correlated across sources to produce a single authoritative sequence. The timeline is the foundation of the rest of the postmortem: the causes are identified by analyzing what happened in the timeline, the action items address specific weaknesses the timeline reveals, and the metric for the postmortem's quality (time-to-detect, time-to-mitigate, time-to-resolve) is computed from the timeline's timestamps. The discipline is to reconstruct the timeline from evidence rather than memory — engineers' recollections of an incident are notoriously unreliable (stress, sleep deprivation, confirmation bias), and the timeline must be anchored in logs and metrics that cannot be misremembered.

The fifth concept is correlation versus causation. During an incident, dozens of metrics deviate from baseline, and the temptation is to seize on the most obvious deviation as the cause. The postmortem's job is to distinguish correlation (two things happened at the same time) from causation (one thing caused the other). The example: an incident where database CPU spiked, request latency spiked, and error rate spiked simultaneously. The correlation is clear; the causation is not — did the CPU spike cause the latency, which caused the errors? Or did a slow query cause both latency and CPU spike (the database working hard to execute the slow query)? The postmortem must establish causation through evidence: query logs showing the slow query began before the CPU spike, EXPLAIN plans showing a full table scan, schema changes showing a missing index. The discipline is to never infer causation from correlation alone; require a causal mechanism backed by evidence. The failure mode is the "post hoc ergo propter hoc" fallacy — "B happened after A, therefore A caused B" — which produces postmortems that fix the wrong thing.

The real-world example is the AWS 2017 us-east-1 outage, where an engineer's typo in a debugging command took down S3 in the entire us-east-1 region for four hours, cascading to thousands of dependent services. The RCA, published publicly, is a model of blameless postmortem practice: it identifies the proximate cause (the typo'd command removed more servers than intended), contributing causes (the subsystem had not been fully tested with the new command, capacity was below the safety threshold, the index subsystem took longer to restart than expected), and systemic causes (the CLI allowed a dangerous operation without a confirmation prompt, capacity was not provisioned to handle the loss of more than one index server). The action items were concrete and tracked: add confirmation prompts to dangerous commands, provision capacity for N+2 failures, change the index subsystem's restart behavior, and add a service-health dashboard. The RCA did not name or blame the engineer; it treated the incident as a system-level failure that the engineer happened to trigger. AWS's public RCA culture, dating to the 2011 ELB outage, has made blameless postmortems the industry standard for major incidents.

The trade-off in RCA is thoroughness versus timeliness. A thorough postmortem takes weeks (interview every participant, correlate every log, test every hypothesis), during which the team's attention is diverted from new feature work and the system remains vulnerable to recurrence. A timely postmortem takes days (timeline, obvious causes, immediate action items), but may miss deeper systemic causes. The state of the art is a two-phase process: a quick (24–48 hour) postmortem that captures the timeline, the obvious causes, and the immediate action items, followed by a deeper (1–2 week) analysis that tests hypotheses, identifies systemic causes, and produces longer-term action items. The two-phase approach captures learning while it is fresh and produces depth without blocking the team's roadmap. The discipline is to always do the quick postmortem, even for minor incidents, and to escalate to the deep postmortem for major incidents or for patterns of minor incidents that suggest a systemic weakness.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Incident mitigated] --> B[48h: quick postmortem]
    B --> C[Reconstruct timeline from logs/metrics/chat]
    C --> D[Identify causes: 5 Whys + fishbone]
    D --> E[Distinguish correlation vs causation]
    E --> F[Action items with owners + due dates]
    F --> G[2wk: deep analysis for systemic causes]
    G --> H[Publish blameless postmortem]
    H --> I[Track action items to completion]
    I --> J[Review at quarterly postmortem-of-postmortem]
    J --> A
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
Incident mitigated
        |
        v
+---------------------------+
| Phase 1: Quick (24-48h)   |
+---------------------------+
  | 1. Reconstruct timeline (logs, metrics, chat, on-call notes)
  | 2. Identify proximate cause (what triggered it)
  | 3. Identify contributing causes (what made it worse)
  | 4. Immediate action items (owners, due dates)
  v
+---------------------------+
| Phase 2: Deep (1-2 weeks) |
+---------------------------+
  | 5. 5 Whys from symptom to systemic root
  | 6. Fishbone across categories (People/Process/Tech/Env)
  | 7. Test hypotheses (reproduce in staging)
  | 8. Distinguish correlation from causation (evidence-backed)
  | 9. Longer-term action items (architectural, process)
  v
+---------------------------+
| Blameless postmortem doc  |
+---------------------------+
  | - Timeline (timestamped, evidence-backed)
  | - Causes (multiple, not "the" cause)
  | - Action items (SMART: specific, measurable, assigned, time-bound)
  | - Metrics: TTD, TTM, TTR (detect/mitigate/resolve)
  v
+---------------------------+
| Track actions to done     |  <- quarterly review
+---------------------------+  <- postmortem-of-postmortem
```

### Walkthrough
1. After the incident is mitigated, the team opens a quick postmortem within 24–48 hours to capture the timeline (from logs, metrics, chat transcripts, on-call notes) while memory is fresh.
2. The team applies 5 Whys to walk from the symptom (user-visible harm) to the proximate cause and on to the systemic root, stopping only when the answer is a system-level weakness.
3. The team uses a fishbone diagram to surface contributing causes across categories (People, Process, Technology, Environment), ensuring breadth rather than fixating on the obvious cause.
4. The team distinguishes correlation from causation by requiring a causal mechanism backed by evidence (logs, EXPLAIN plans, repro in staging), not just temporal coincidence.
5. Action items are SMART (specific, measurable, assigned, time-bound), tracked to completion, and reviewed quarterly in a postmortem-of-postmortem to improve the RCA process itself.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Time-to-detect in minutes (first event to first alert).
- Rca_template.py - runnable; postmortem template generator with timeline + 5 Whys

**Defines:** `Severity`, `ActionState`, `TimelineEvent`, `WhyStep`, `ActionItem`, `Postmortem`

```python
# rca_template.py - runnable; postmortem template generator with timeline + 5 Whys
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime
from enum import Enum

class Severity(Enum):
    SEV1 = "sev1"   # full outage, user-visible
    SEV2 = "sev2"   # partial degradation, user-visible
    SEV3 = "sev3"   # internal, no user impact

class ActionState(Enum):
    OPEN = "open"
    IN_PROGRESS = "in_progress"
    DONE = "done"

@dataclass
class TimelineEvent:
    timestamp: str
    source: str          # "log", "metric", "chat", "on-call"
    description: str
    evidence_link: str = ""

@dataclass
class WhyStep:
    question: str
    answer: str
    evidence: str        # what proves this answer

@dataclass
class ActionItem:
    description: str
    owner: str
    due_date: str
    state: ActionState = ActionState.OPEN
    prevents_class: str = ""   # what class of incidents this prevents

@dataclass
class Postmortem:
    title: str
    severity: Severity
    incident_start: str        # ISO timestamp
    mitigated_at: str
    resolved_at: str
    summary: str
    timeline: list[TimelineEvent] = field(default_factory=list)
    five_whys: list[WhyStep] = field(default_factory=list)
    contributing_causes: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    action_items: list[ActionItem] = field(default_factory=list)
    blameless: bool = True     # enforce no individual blame

    def ttd(self) -> int:
        """Time-to-detect in minutes (first event to first alert)."""
        return 0  # computed from timeline in practice

    def render(self) -> str:
        out = [f"# Postmortem: {self.title}\n"]
        out.append(f"Severity: {self.severity.value} | Blameless: {self.blameless}\n")
        out.append(f"## Summary\n{self.summary}\n")
        out.append("## Timeline")
        for e in self.timeline:
            out.append(f"  - [{e.timestamp}] ({e.source}) {e.description}")
        out.append("\n## 5 Whys (symptom -> systemic root)")
        for i, w in enumerate(self.five_whys, 1):
            out.append(f"  {i}. Q: {w.question}")
            out.append(f"     A: {w.answer}")
            out.append(f"     Evidence: {w.evidence}")
        out.append("\n## Contributing Causes")
        for c in self.contributing_causes:
            out.append(f"  - {c}")
        out.append("\n## Action Items")
        for a in self.action_items:
            out.append(f"  - [{a.state.value}] {a.description} "
                       f"(owner: {a.owner}, due: {a.due_date})")
            if a.prevents_class:
                out.append(f"    prevents class: {a.prevents_class}")
        return "\n".join(out)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    pm = Postmortem(
        title="S3 us-east-1 outage (example structure)",
        severity=Severity.SEV1,
        incident_start="2017-02-28T09:37:00Z",
        mitigated_at="2017-02-28T13:30:00Z",
        resolved_at="2017-02-28T14:10:00Z",
        summary="A typo in a debugging command removed too many index servers, "
                "taking S3 offline in us-east-1 for ~4 hours.",
    )
    pm.timeline = [
        TimelineEvent("09:37", "on-call", "Engineer ran `playback` command with wrong arg"),
        TimelineEvent("09:38", "metric", "S3 error rate spiked to 100% in us-east-1"),
        TimelineEvent("09:39", "alert", "SLO burn-rate alert fired, paged on-call"),
        TimelineEvent("09:45", "chat", "On-call declared SEV1, opened incident bridge"),
        TimelineEvent("13:30", "metric", "Index subsystems fully restarted, S3 recovered"),
    ]
    pm.five_whys = [
        WhyStep("Why did S3 go down?",
                "The index subsystem lost capacity below the safety threshold.",
                "Capacity dashboard showing index servers dropping to <required"),
        WhyStep("Why did capacity drop below threshold?",
                "A debugging command removed more servers than intended.",
                "Command audit log showing the typo'd argument"),
        WhyStep("Why did the command remove too many servers?",
                "The CLI accepted the dangerous arg without a confirmation prompt.",
                "CLI source code showing no confirmation for this operation"),
        WhyStep("Why was there no confirmation prompt?",
                "The CLI was designed for internal debugging and trusted the operator.",
                "Design doc from CLI's original release"),
        WhyStep("Why was the CLI trusted despite the operation's blast radius?",
                "No process existed for reviewing CLI commands against blast radius.",
                "Process audit showing no such review step in CLI release"),
    ]
    pm.contributing_causes = [
        "Capacity was provisioned for N+1, not N+2, so single human error was fatal",
        "Index subsystem took ~4h to restart, far longer than expected",
        "Service-health dashboard did not exist, slowing diagnosis for dependent services",
    ]
    pm.action_items = [
        ActionItem("Add confirmation prompt to dangerous CLI commands",
                   "cli-team", "2017-03-15", prevents_class="operator-error-commands"),
        ActionItem("Provision index capacity to N+2",
                   "storage-capacity", "2017-04-01",
                   prevents_class="single-error-capacity-loss"),
        ActionItem("Publish service-health dashboard for dependent services",
                   "status-team", "2017-03-30",
                   prevents_class="dependent-service-blindness"),
    ]
    print(pm.render())
```
